en: The Essential Ritual for Using the Three Waters,
composed by the Tripitaka Master Yijing of the Tang Dynasty.
Based upon the holy teachings and according to the water currently used by sentient beings in the Western Regions, there are...
There are three distinctions:
first, water at the proper time;
second, water not at the proper time.
Third is the water for touching.
Regarding the term "water for the time," this refers to śrāmaṇeras and laypeople.
One should strain the water with one's own hand,
observe it to ensure there are no insects, and then consume it before noon.
If the water has been touched by the hands of the *saṃgha*— whether from the basin, the filter, or the ladle— it is unfit for consumption.
How much more so regarding food and drink;
because they involve unwholesome contact, they are just like the water commonly used by the Saṃgha—
how could a Great Bhikṣu ever touch it?
Although the great monks do not touch it,
it is improper to drink or use it during the afternoon;
however, as for the substance of water itself, it is untouchable.
Since it has already been touched by laypeople and others,
it carries defilement and is not entirely pure;
therefore, one must accept it.
Regarding the second point, "purified water at improper times":
this refers to great bhikṣus, śrāmaṇeras, and others who are responsible for such matters;
they must all have soap powder (*śāṭī*) and fine ash, among other things.
The four fingers of both hands must be thoroughly washed until they are free of any grime or oiliness;
the earthen basin and the strainer must also be brand new and clean.
It can only be obtained by one who is not defiled by impurities.
This water must be filtered using exclusively copper bowls and copper ladles.
One must first scrub away the grease with ash before one may take water.
If such things cannot be found,
there must certainly be a wooden vessel for dyeing.
It has never been defiled by contact with oily substances;
it may be used for general purposes as well, provided it is washed daily until all dust and grime have been removed without ceasing.
If one regularly uses water, it may be stored in a pure vessel (*śuci-ghaṭa*).
This pure vessel must be made of earthenware;
it is not a copper *kuṇḍikā* (bathing pitcher).
Because there was impure copper-green (copper sulfate) inside the jar that could not be removed by rubbing with ash,
he pulled out a copper hairpin and rubbed it;
thus he immediately knew whether it was clean or defiled.
However, it is explicitly stated in the holy teachings that copper is purified by scrubbing it with ash;
if one washes it with soap powder (kṣāra), [it is not so].
Simply go and eat something greasy;
the copper stain will not be removed,
so you may take a copper spoon and scrub it with ash.
This serves as a direct verification:
when the water in the earthen jar is exhausted,
it must always be washed out before fresh water can be poured in.
However, throughout the lands of the Five Indias,
there is no one who uses a copper vessel as a *kamaṇḍalu*;
this is because impurities arise from it and it becomes defiled by contact.
Second, copper has a metallic odor that harms people.
This pure water may be taken for drinking at any time, whether it be the proper time or otherwise,
according to one's inclination.
This is a special provision made by the Buddha; because it is pure,
one need not undergo the formal reception again.
If a bhikṣu, during the improper time,
boils medicine, brews tea, or prepares honey-drinks and the like, he must use this water;
he must not use the water from the previous [proper] time.
Because they involve faults,
however, one must ensure that spears, ladles, bowls,
and other utensils are all kept free from the defilement of food.
Furthermore, all items used for scrubbing with ash should be boiled together before use.
The clean water basins and jars should be placed in a pure location.
The jar must be covered with a clean cloth;
it should be placed in a bamboo basket and not allowed to be touched by anyone at random.
When wishing to use water, first wash the hands clean;
alternatively, rub the hands thoroughly with dry cow dung until they are purified.
To prevent the liquid from adhering,
one may use a clean silk cloth or leaves to replace the neck of the flask.
Only then should one take hold of it.
The Vinaya states:
"With the exception of water and tooth-sticks."
That is to say, this pure water is not either of the other two;
as for the *yāñci* (tooth-stick), it should be a fresh branch that is moist.
One must purify it with fire before accepting and chewing it;
thus, one should know that one cannot simply rely on the literal text of the precepts.
Whenever one intends to place water into the mouth, [one must first purify it].
Whether drinking or rinsing the mouth, whether at the proper time or otherwise,
one must always wash the hands with cleansing powder (kṣāra) and thoroughly cleanse both lips;
only after rinsing the mouth twice or thrice is it appropriate to drink water.
The same applies to eating.
Furthermore, when the midday meal is finished,
if one fears that the water in the purification flask (*parisrāvaṇa*) may be insufficient:
One must have a layperson offer the aforementioned water;
after chewing the tooth-stick and rinsing the mouth,
one must not swallow the saliva prematurely.
One must first rinse the mouth three times with this pure water;
only then is one purified enough to swallow the saliva in the mouth.

I have personally witnessed the monastic community in the western region of the Southern Sea practicing this method together, and there were also ancient virtuous Vinaya masters in this land who were aware of this matter.
However, those who practice this are rare.
If one does not do so,
the remaining grease will not be removed, and one will incur an offense with every swallow.
Furthermore, the fast is not accomplished.
Regarding the three types of water that come into contact [with the body]:
it simply requires that there be no insects.
Regardless of whether it is pure or impure, one may immediately make use of it;
that is, one may take the water-jar containing the added water to the places for defecation and urination,
as well as for washing the hands and feet.
Furthermore, one must not casually take these remaining waters into the mouth,
much less consume them as food.
One should know through the three types of water-contemplation that they are free of insects.
Until the appearance of the dawn has not yet emerged,
one may use [the items] according to their respective purposes;
once the appearance of the dawn has emerged, it is no longer appropriate to do so, regardless of how many there may be.
Even down to a single scoop from within a jar or a single handful from within a basin,
one must use a copper cup and observe with clear eyes.
If there are no insects,
one may use it for many days without committing an offense.
Among the monastic community and laypeople of the Western Regions, the five precepts are regarded as the most urgent.
If visiting monks from other regions do not understand this method of purification through water and contact,
they are not permitted to enter the monastery.
Furthermore, such is the monastic custom in the West.
If one sees a monk who, having taken a ritual water jar (kamaṇḍalu) to the latrine, drinks from the water that has been touched there,
considering this to be the destruction of the Dharma,
one should immediately expel him from the monastery.
Speaking thus,
I hope that all practitioners will together provide protection and guardianship.
This will cause the Buddha-dharma to abide for a long time.
If one can practice according to the teachings,
it is no different from the Buddha being present in the world.
Furthermore, the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* (Ten Recitations), fascicle 59, states:
"There are pure water jars and toilet water jars.
Fascicle 41 states: [same].
There is the *śikya* (water-purifying vessel) and the *nitya-śikya* (constant water vessel).
Furthermore, in the newly translated Vinaya texts of the Sarvāstivāda school,
the distinction between the *śikya* and the vessel used for touching [impure objects] is extremely clear.
These are all the direct words from the Buddha’s own mouth,
not human fabrications.
How could it be permissible for there to be only a single copper vessel that is neither pure nor defiled?
Although they may speak the same words, they do not take them to heart;
how can one disregard the sacred teachings merely because of long-standing custom and habitual practice?
According to this principle:
In the rooms of various monasteries and in places where people travel,
the use of water is extremely disorganized;
it is sometimes kept in large basins.
Alternatively, if they are kept in jars or placed inside flasks,
these are all unsuitable for use;
for it is improper for a fully ordained monk to touch them with his hands or to strain water through them.
If it has been left overnight without inspection,
and has been stored for a long time, there will certainly be living beings present;
even if there are no insects, [one must still exercise caution].
Drinking the third portion of water constitutes an offense;
this is because it has been touched by hands that are impure due to contact with a strainer or a ladle, and thus contains impure particles.
It is also like the case of an ordinary copper water-jar used for water.
If one drinks by taking it up oneself,
because it is impure and has not been received, there is the offense of drinking what has not been received.
If one touches [the substance] before midday and drinks it after noon,
one incurs an offense of *atireka-saṃsarga*.
If one touches it today and drinks it tomorrow, [one likewise incurs an offense].
There is the offense of prior contact;
there is the offense of grasping without having received [permission];
and there is the offense of improper contact.
Not washing one's hands clean;
furthermore, there is the offense of grasping a drinking vessel with defiled hands;
and drinking water without having rinsed the lips and mouth clean.
There are impure offenses.
These six offenses each have preparatory stages, which together constitute twelve offenses.
All incur the offense of disrespecting the holy teaching.
This has twenty-four underlying causes.
Adding these to the previous, they constitute thirty-six offenses.
If one conceals them for a night,
there are further seventy-two offenses based on the original causes.
Adding to the previous one hundred and eight offenses,
if one does not study these,
there are two further offenses: that of failing to study and that of ignorance.
Furthermore, there are four hundred and thirty-two offenses established based on their origins;
added to the previous total, they constitute five hundred and forty offenses.
Moreover, starting from the concealment [of offenses] and below...
Furthermore, those who do not study and lack knowledge all possess the fundamental roots of disrespecting the teachings and expedient means;
there are additionally one thousand and eight offenses.
Adding the previous five hundred and forty,
there are one thousand five hundred and forty offenses in total.
These figures are based on a brief calculation of the number of offenses arising from a single swallow and a single night's stay.
If one calculates the offenses incurred from ten suppressions over a single night,
there are fifteen thousand four hundred and eighty;
if they are concealed for a long period, offenses are generated in succession.
Until they have been confessed,
those whose number is unknown or who are grave must all confess and repent before a pure person.
If one knows [the time] beforehand, there is no fault of ignorance.
If one drinks salt broth or honey syrup at an improper time,
one should use a ladle, a spoon, or a bowl, and strain the water with a water filter.
It was not prepared according to the Dharma;
it was either contaminated by oily substances or came into contact with food that may be eaten at the proper time.
If the hands or mouth are impure, one must not receive offerings with palms turned upward;
doing so in either case constitutes an offense. Furthermore, apricot seed tea and hot water are not consumed in the Western Regions.
If it is within a monastery, one must personally inspect it;
if it is in a layperson's home, one must inquire in detail to ascertain whether it is pure.
If it is not in accordance with the Dharma, one must not drink it.
How can one endure long-term suffering in the future for the sake of what the mouth and belly require for a mere moment?
We all know that the Elāpattra dragon once damaged a single leaf [for this reason].
Even now, one has not yet escaped the time of non-recollection;
how much less could this constant state constitute a path of action?
It is like swallowing a single mouthful of food.
The offenses are indeed boundless;
to bear this burden for the rest of one's life is truly pitiable.
Therefore, the Sūtra says:
"Do not underestimate a minor transgression, thinking it will bring no calamity.
It further says: "Carefully protect the life-preserving skin bag, guarding against even the slightest leak."
The intent of both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna is the same in this regard.
This provides a brief account of the essential practices;
the remainder is as set forth in the Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra.
May all practitioners,
in accordance with the holy teachings,
perform the essential ritual for the reception and enjoyment of the three waters.
